title: Hussain-lab-05
text:
The NMES1988 data describe 4,406 adults aged 66 and older from the 1987–1988 US National Medical Expenditure Survey. It details several variables with the outcome variable being number of physician office visits. The rest are listed below

The visits outcome is a count. Whole numbers, bounded at zero, and right-skewed. The variance (45.69) is about 7.91 times the mean (5.77). 16% of people had no visits. The greatest number of visits reported (89)is a shockingly large number, but could be legitimate.









A linear model is a poor choice for the visits outcome variable because the visits data are counts, meaning that negative visits and half visits are impossible/meaningless values. This is evidenced by the DHARMa simulations. The residuals, shown in the QQ plot, do not follow the expected flat diagonal line. The outlier and KS tests also speak to this concern. In the residual-vs-predicted plot, as the predicted probability approaches 1, the distribution becomes more compressed toward the lower end of residual values. This is also evidenced by the red 0.5 quantile line. Taken together, its clear these data are not a good fit for a Gaussian model.

For the comparison between M0 and M1, nested χ² = 2,175.428, p <.001. For the comparison between M1 and M2, nested χ² = 959.924, p <.001. Both of these likelihood-ratio tests indicate a statistically significant improvement in model fit. This means that adding the additional predictors improved the model fit across both comparisons, suggesting that M2 is a better fit model than M1 and M0. Further, the AIC and BIC decreased for both comparisons, once again implying that M2 is a good model to select. For these reasons, I have selected M2 as the ideal model.
The provisionally selected model is M2: Full.

    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 15.035, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


The DHARMa plots suggest that the Poisson model is a poor fit. The dispersion ratio is 7.25 (p < .001), and there are 15.03 times as many zeros as the Poisson expects. The observed data are more variable than a Poisson allows.
The over dispersion observed here matters because it means that the assumption that the variance is equal to the mean has been violated. In this case the variance is underestimated, meaning that model’s standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals are too narrow, and the p-values are too small. I would not move straight to a zero-inflated model based on this zero-inflation test alone because the test only tells me that there are more zeros than the Poisson expects, it does not tell me if these zeros are coming from structural reasons (i.e. some people have no reason to visit a doctor during this period). Whether the zeros are structural or not will define if I should move to a zero-inflated model.

The negative binomial model fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(1) = 1.212908^{4}, p < .001.
This test has 1 degree of freedom because the negative binomial model adds more more layer of complexity by adding one parameter that describes the extra variability in the data. Yes, the NB2 fit significantly better than the Poisson. This is evidenced by the large reduction in AIC and BIC and the significance of the LRT test. This tells us that adding complexity to the model didn’t take away from the significance of the relationship. The NB2 resolved our over dispersion issue, but our issue of excess zero may remain.

























The NB resolved the over dispersion: the dispersion ratio is now 1.04 (p = 0.432), close to 1 and non-significant.









The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors because of the the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount on the log scale, multiplying the expected count, so the same one-condition increase adds more visits when the expected count is already high.

Part 5: Do the zeros need their own model?
Given that my NB2 zero-inflation test produced a significant result, I will test ZINB and Hurdle NB models to see if the fit is improved and the zero-inflation is resolved.

I will carry forward the hurdle negative binomial model for a few reasons. Initially, the ZINB-full model was found to fit significantly better than the ordinary negative binomial model. This was a good first step of providing evidence that adding the zero-inflation component improves the model.The DHARMa result for the ZINB-full model was ratioObsSim = 0.95671, p = 0.176. The p being > .05, indicated there was no statistically significant evidence of remaining zero inflation. I then conducted the same test for the hurdle model and found that the results were ratioObsSim = 0.99928, p = 1. Since p > .05 again, this meant that there was no statistically significant evidence of remaining zero inflation for the hurdle model either. Because both the ZINB-full and hurdle models passed the DHARMa zero-inflation test, the decision for which model to select is now based on the AIC/BIC comparison of the two model options. The comparison showed that the hurdle model had the lowest AIC (24,330.41) and BIC (24,426.27) of all four models. Thus, I choose to carry forward the hurdle model.


Part 6: Testing and probing an interaction
Question: Does the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differ for people based on gender?
I predict that the association between number of chronic conditions and physician visits differs for male and female patients such that female patients will have a weaker association between the predictor and the outcome variable. My thinking here is that female health is not well understood in many domains, so while a female patients may be attending many visits to the doctor, they may not be able to report an accurate number of chronic conditions due to the fact that physicians may not provide adequate diagnoses. This would probably be especially true for female patients in the window of time we are examining (1987–1988).
